They brought in another group of refugees today. As unsettling as the Kryptis are to look at, you adjust to that when you start talking to them, as they're surprisingly intelligent.

Normally, that is. But today's batch was all these little ones, just a flood of teeth and claws. When we set out food for them, they tore through it so aggressively that I genuinely worried they would eat the table as well. When they were done, it was as though a swarm of locusts had passed by, picking every last scrap of anything even resembling food.

They thanked us afterward though, in that same awkward way that they say everything else. Once the hunger was gone, there was only gratitude. They had been certain they were going to die, and now they follow us around the camp like rescued pups. I can't help but feel sorry for them.

More detailed examinations made of the key structures today. The style shares similarities with the few other seer examples we have, but while those showed evidence of integration with other early Tyrian cultures, the designs here are truly unique. It'll take time to ascertain their precise age, but it looks like these really do predate everything else we've found before.  
 
And yet, they appear even more complex and detailed than the structures that came later. This suggests a decline in craftsmanship, but why? Possible theories: 
 
1. The mainland examples represent a divergent group of seers who broke off and lived separately and thus developed a different culture.  
  
2. The mainland examples we've found were from a remnant of the overall culture that survived for an undetermined period after the destruction of their civilization.  
  
3. The mainland examples are really just evidence of non-seers adapting the ruins for their own purposes.  
  
Further study will be needed to determine which of these hypotheses is most likely.
